title: The History of Machine Learning
description: Key historical discoveries, foundational concepts, and eras in the evolution of machine learning and artificial intelligence.

events.title: Bayes' Theorem
events.description: Thomas Bayes' theorem and its predecessors laid foundational statistical methods that underlie inference, describing the probability of an event occurring based on prior knowledge.

events.title: Least Squares Theory
events.description: Introduced by French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre, this theory provides a standard approach in regression analysis for data fitting by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.

events.title: Markov Chains
events.description: Named after Russian mathematician Andrey Markov, these stochastic models describe a sequence of possible events where the probability of each event depends only on the state attained in the previous event.

events.title: Turing Test & Thinking Machines
events.description: Alan Turing helped lay the foundation for artificial intelligence and proposed the Turing Test to empirically evaluate whether a machine can exhibit intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human.

events.title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project
events.description: A seminal event organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon where the term 'artificial intelligence' was officially coined.

events.title: The Perceptron
events.description: Invented by American psychologist Frank Rosenblatt, the Perceptron is an early type of linear classifier that laid crucial groundwork for modern deep learning architectures.

events.title: The Golden Years of AI
events.description: A period of high optimism where AI research flourished in natural language processing and search, driven by the belief that intelligent machines could soon be fully realized.

events.title: The First AI Winter
events.description: Optimism slowed and funding dried up as researchers confronted severe limitations including lack of computing power, combinatorial explosion of parameters, and data scarcity.
